strengths: The task addresses a useful capability: retrieving a person using both a reference image and a description of appearance changes, without training on composed-query triplets. ITCPR provides a potentially valuable benchmark with 2,202 queries and 20,510 gallery images drawn from three datasets.

The reported improvements over simple fusion are substantial and consistent across two backbones. With ViT-L/14, Word4Per achieves 45.549% Rank-1 and 55.260% mAP, versus 32.016% and 41.831% for fine-tuned image–text feature averaging.

The two-stage pipeline is understandable and practical. Extensive ablations examine supervision, training-data volume, network architecture, vocabulary substitution, and ensemble inference. Training hyperparameters and supplementary timing results aid reproduction, and the absence of explicit facial/body consistency modeling is acknowledged honestly.
weaknesses: The headline comparison with prior methods is confounded. Table 1 explicitly acknowledges that Pic2Word’s mapper was trained with original CLIP parameters but is evaluated with fine-tuned encoders. This disadvantages the comparator through an embedding-space mismatch. Table 2 provides a useful partial control on ViT-B/16, but an equivalent comparison for the headline ViT-L/14 setting is missing. The cited textual-inversion method of Baldrati et al. [2] is also not evaluated.

Methodological originality is limited: the image-to-pseudo-word mapper closely follows Pic2Word, while encoder adaptation and matching objectives largely reuse existing person-retrieval techniques. The application and benchmark are the clearest contributions; the paper does not sufficiently establish what generalizable methodological insight goes beyond combining these components.

The evaluation protocol leaves model-selection bias unresolved. ITCPR is designated exclusively for testing, yet the supplement selects optimal network architectures, training subsets, and fusion configurations using its results without describing an independent validation procedure. Repeated-run variability or confidence intervals are also absent, weakening conclusions about smaller ablation and ensemble gains.

The benchmark needs stronger validation because it carries much of the contribution. Model-assisted screening for missed positives is useful, but annotation agreement, screening depth, and residual missed-positive rates are not reported. Results are pooled across the three source datasets, and there is no systematic breakdown by clothing-change severity. Deliberately selecting pairs with overlapping clothing limits evidence for broader identity preservation under appearance changes.

Some explanatory claims exceed the experiments. The conclusion that data quality outweighs quantity confounds resolution filtering, dataset composition, annotation style, and domain alignment; matched-size controls are needed. Nearest-vocabulary examples likewise suggest semantic associations but do not establish reliable disentanglement or compositional control.

The proposed release of person imagery and explicit surveillance motivation warrant documentation of redistribution permissions, consent/privacy handling, and potential misuse. These are not addressed adequately. This is a material documentation gap, rather than evidence by itself of an ethical violation.
